L'AQUILA, Italy (CNN) -- The youngest hadn't lived half a year. The oldest had lived nearly a hundred. A rescue worker Friday kisses the coffin of a child killed by this week's earthquake in central Italy. The official government list of victims from this week's earthquake in central Italy reached 287 on Friday, as Italians held a mass state funeral to lay the victims to rest. They included Antonio Loavan Ghiroceanu, who was born December 11. He would have been  6 months old on Saturday. The oldest-known victim of the quake was Evandro Testa, 96, who was born in 1913. More than 200 caskets were lined up at the funeral, draped with flowers. At least one small white coffin belonging to a child sat atop a larger coffin, a baby's pastel outfit hanging off the side. The funeral was being held outside a hangar in Coppito, a town adjacent to the earthquake's epicenter of L'Aquila. Officials elected to hold the Mass in the open air to avoid the risk of injury from falling debris. Aftershocks continue to shake the region more than four days after the earthquake, and some were even felt during Friday's funeral. All of the area's cardinals and bishops, along with 100 priests, attended the special funeral Mass. Italian Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi was also there, greeting and embracing some of the thousands of mourners before the service. Cardinal Tarcisio Bertone presided over the Mass as an envoy from Pope Benedict XVI, who plans to visit the region after Easter.  Watch Italy bury its dead » . Bertone said the funeral was a "precious moment" to understand the meaning of life and death. "Everything can stop in a second -- projects, plans -- everything finishes. All that remains is love," he said. Watch more on funeral . Mourners, who were transported to the funeral on buses, dabbed their eyes and noses. Some stared at the ground or held each other. Few appeared focused on anything but remembering the victims. "I feel rebirth in the heart, because below that rubble there is a will to rebuild, to start again, to plan and to dream," Bertone said, offering a message of hope. The towns of L'Aquila and the surrounding region, he said, "will come back stronger, will have more courage and give life to these places with that power and strength and dignity of the soul that distinguishes them." As well as sending Bertone to deliver his message, the pope sent holy oils to L'Aquila and a chalice with which to take Communion. Archbishop Giuseppe Molinari of L'Aquila also planned to deliver a message. The 6.3-magnitude quake Monday morning left about 30,000 people without their homes. Almost 20,000 of them are braving chilly nights in tents while about 11,000 others are staying in hotels, said Agostino Miozzo, a spokesman for the Italian Civil Protection Agency. Watch more on the aftermath . Recovering from such losses and rebuilding the city of L'Aquila will take several years, according to Miozzo. The medieval city is about 120 km (75 miles) northeast of Rome. Berlusconi has said rebuilding will cost several billion euros. Aftershocks have heightened anxiety in the area -- including a moderate 5.6 magnitude tremor that struck the area Tuesday. "The mood is a little bit afraid," said Marco Volponi of the Civil Protection agency. He was working in a tent camp, housing people whose homes were inhabitable. In the nearby village of Onna, 40 people -- more than one out of every eight residents in the town of 300 -- were killed in the earthquake. On some streets, every single home was destroyed. Anna Rita Difilice lost her son, Fabio, 20, to the quake -- the deadliest to strike Italy in decades and the first major quake in the country in seven years. She said she doesn't know what comes next for her. Her village has become populated with tents, fold-up beds and feeding stations handing out food, water and other supplies for survivors. But she said she knew one thing: she's not going anywhere. "My son died here," she said. "There is no way I'm leaving this town -- not ever."

outputs.L1:
L'AQUILA, Italy (CNN) -- The youngest had not yet lived half a year. The oldest had lived nearly a century. On Friday, a rescue worker knelt to kiss the coffin of a child killed in this week's earthquake in central Italy.

The official government death toll from this week's earthquake reached 287 on Friday, as Italians gathered for a mass state funeral to lay the victims to rest. Among them was Antonio Loavan Ghiroceanu, born December 11, who would have turned six months old on Saturday. The oldest known victim was Evandro Testa, 96, born in 1913.

More than 200 caskets, draped in flowers, were arranged in solemn rows at the funeral. At least one small white coffin belonging to a child rested atop a larger casket, a baby's pastel outfit draped poignantly over its side.

The funeral was held in the open air outside a hangar in Coppito, a town near L'Aquila, the earthquake's epicenter. Officials chose an outdoor venue to minimize the risk of injury from falling debris, as aftershocks continued to shake the region more than four days after the initial quake—some tremors felt even during Friday's service.

All of the region's cardinals and bishops, along with 100 priests, attended the solemn Mass. Italian Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi was also present, greeting and embracing mourners among the thousands who had gathered before the service began.

Cardinal Tarcisio Bertone presided over the Mass as an envoy of Pope Benedict XVI, who intends to visit the region after Easter. Bertone described the funeral as a "precious moment" for reflecting on the meaning of life and death. "Everything can stop in a second—projects, plans—everything finishes. All that remains is love," he said.

Mourners, transported to the service by bus, wiped away tears as they stared at the ground or embraced one another, their thoughts consumed by memories of the dead.

Yet amid the grief, Bertone offered words of hope: "I feel rebirth in the heart, because beneath that rubble there is a will to rebuild, to start anew, to plan and to dream." He added that L'Aquila and its surrounding towns "will come back stronger, will have more courage, and will give life to these places with that power, strength, and dignity of soul that distinguishes them."

In addition to sending Bertone as his representative, the pope sent holy oils to L'Aquila along with a chalice for Communion. Archbishop Giuseppe Molinari of L'Aquila was also scheduled to deliver a message.

Monday morning's magnitude 6.3 earthquake left roughly 30,000 people homeless. Nearly 20,000 are now enduring cold nights in tents, while about 11,000 others have found shelter in hotels, according to Agostino Miozzo, a spokesman for the Italian Civil Protection Agency.

Rebuilding L'Aquila and recovering from such devastating losses will take years, Miozzo said. The medieval city lies roughly 120 kilometers (75 miles) northeast of Rome, and Berlusconi has estimated that reconstruction will cost several billion euros.

Ongoing aftershocks—including a magnitude 5.6 tremor on Tuesday—have only heightened residents' anxiety. "The mood is a little bit afraid," said Marco Volponi of the Civil Protection Agency, who was working at a tent camp housing those whose homes had been rendered uninhabitable.

In the nearby village of Onna, 40 people—more than one in eight of its 300 residents—were killed in the earthquake. On some streets, not a single home remained standing.

Anna Rita Difilice lost her 20-year-old son, Fabio, in the quake—the deadliest to strike Italy in decades and the country's first major earthquake in seven years. She admitted she did not know what the future held for her, as her village filled with tents, folding beds, and stations distributing food, water, and other essential supplies to survivors.

But of one thing, she remained certain: she would not leave. "My son died here," she said. "There is no way I'm leaving this town—not ever."

# In the Shadow of Ruins: L'Aquila Buries Its Dead

**L'AQUILA, Italy** — The medieval city that once stood as a jewel of the Abruzzo region now lies in fractured silence, its cracked bell towers and collapsed facades bearing witness to the violence that struck in the early morning hours. Today, that silence was broken by the sound of collective mourning, as thousands gathered to bury the dead.

## A City Mourns Together

In a cavernous exhibition hall on the outskirts of the shattered city center—the only space large enough to accommodate the scale of loss—rows of simple wooden coffins stretched across the floor. Some were heartbreakingly small. Mourners dressed in black moved between them, many clutching photographs, others simply standing in stunned silence before caskets bearing the names of neighbors, colleagues, and in the cruelest cases, entire families wiped out in seconds.

The state funeral, attended by government officials and religious leaders, offered little comfort against the enormity of the tragedy. Prayers were read aloud, echoing off the hall's high ceilings, as survivors—many still wearing the same clothes they'd fled in days earlier—wept for loved ones who had been sleeping when the earth convulsed beneath them.

"We buried our history along with our people," one elderly resident was heard saying, gesturing toward the ruins of the city's historic quarter, where centuries-old buildings had crumbled into rubble within seconds.

## The Toll Continues to Climb

Rescue workers, aided by sniffer dogs and heavy machinery, continued combing through the debris of collapsed apartment buildings, dormitories, and homes. With each passing hour, hope of finding survivors diminished, and the death toll—already devastating—continued its grim ascent. Emergency officials cautioned that the number would likely rise further as crews reached areas previously inaccessible due to unstable structures.

Among the dead were students crushed in a collapsed university dormitory, entire families buried in their sleep, and elderly residents who had lived their whole lives in homes that had stood for generations before crumbling in an instant.

## Tent Cities Rise Where Homes Once Stood

Beyond the immediate horror of the death toll lies a slower-unfolding crisis: tens of thousands left without shelter. Makeshift tent camps have sprung up in parks, sports fields, and open lots surrounding the city, transforming into temporary villages for a population suddenly rendered homeless.

Inside these canvas shelters, families huddle together, uncertain of what comes next. Blankets, cots, and donated clothing offer scant comfort against the psychological weight of displacement. Aid organizations have mobilized to provide food and water, but the scale of need strains resources thin.

"We have nothing to go back to," said one woman outside a crowded tent, her children playing nearby, seemingly unaware of the gravity surrounding them. "Our home doesn't exist anymore. Where do we go from here?"

Local authorities, working alongside national emergency management teams, face the daunting task of not only continuing search and rescue operations but also planning for the long-term housing of a displaced population that may not be able to return to the city center for months, if not years.

## An Uncertain Road Ahead
